learn.title: How it works
learn.intro: Every picture in Mirrorfold is made by arithmetic. There are no drawings in it and no stored shapes. These lessons build the pictures from nothing but multiplying and adding, one small idea at a time. Each step has something to drag, and none of it needs more than school arithmetic. Start with the first track. The others build on it. The last one goes furthest, and is the hardest.
learn.track.mandel: From one number to the Mandelbrot set
learn.voiceFail: The voice for this step could not be played.
learn.figure: Drawing for this step. Drag in it, or use the arrow keys.
learn.mandel.once.title: Multiply a number by itself
learn.mandel.once.text: Pick a number and multiply it by itself. Two times two is four. Three times three is nine. So far that makes numbers bigger. But try a half. Half of a half is a quarter, which is smaller. So multiplying a number by itself does not always make it bigger. Numbers above one grow. Numbers between zero and one shrink. And one stays exactly where it is, because one times one is one.
learn.mandel.once.do: Drag the blue dot. The arch shows where the number lands. Find the two places where a number lands on itself.
learn.mandel.once.name: Multiplying a number by itself is called squaring it, because it gives the area of a square with sides of that length.
learn.mandel.minus.title: Numbers below zero
learn.mandel.minus.text: Now let the number go below zero. Multiply minus two by minus two, and the answer is plus four. A minus times a minus is always a plus. So whichever side of zero a number starts on, it lands on the positive side. Minus a half lands on a quarter, just as a half does.
learn.mandel.minus.do: Drag the dot to the left of zero. Then find two different numbers that land on the same place.
learn.mandel.minus.name: Numbers below zero are called negative numbers. The square of a number on this line is never negative. Keep that in mind. In a few steps we will meet a number whose square is minus one.
learn.mandel.again.title: Do it again, and again
learn.mandel.again.text: Now take the answer and square that. Then square the new answer, and keep going. Each arch is one squaring. Only three things can happen. A number between minus one and one shrinks toward zero. A number further out than that grows faster and faster, and runs away. And a number that starts exactly on one stays put.
learn.mandel.again.do: Drag the dot slowly past one. Watch shrinking turn into running away. Press Next hop to follow the arithmetic one squaring at a time.
learn.mandel.again.name: Doing the same thing over and over, feeding each answer back in, is called iteration. The list of answers is called a sequence. Zero and one are called fixed points, because the rule leaves them where they are.
learn.mandel.addc.title: Add a number after each squaring
learn.mandel.addc.text: Change the rule a little. Choose a number and call it c. Start from zero. Square it, then add c. Square the answer, then add c again, and keep going. The first hop always lands on c itself, because zero squared is zero. After that, the squaring and the adding pull against each other. Sometimes the answers settle down. Sometimes they run away.
learn.mandel.addc.do: Drag the pink marker to change c. Try a half, and watch the answers run away. Then try minus a half, and watch them settle. Press Next hop to follow the arithmetic one hop at a time.
learn.mandel.addc.name: A rule that makes each answer from the one before is called a recurrence. The number c is called a parameter: a number you set once, which changes how the whole rule behaves.
learn.mandel.cycles.title: Answers that never settle and never leave
learn.mandel.cycles.text: Settling down and running away are not the only things that can happen. Set c to minus one. The answers go from zero to minus one, back to zero, back to minus one, for ever. They never settle on one number, and they never run away. Other values of c make the answers visit three places in turn, or four. And for some values, the answers stay close but never repeat at all.
learn.mandel.cycles.do: Press each of the buttons under the slider, and count the places the answers keep returning to. The large dots mark them.
learn.mandel.cycles.name: The path the answers take is called an orbit. An orbit that returns to the same places in the same order is called a cycle, and the number of places is its period. An orbit that stays close but never repeats is called chaotic.
learn.mandel.bar.title: Every c at once
learn.mandel.bar.text: Trying one c at a time is slow. So here is every c at once. Under the line there is a bar. Each point of the bar is one value of c. It is bright if the answers for that c stay close, and dark if they run away. The bright part runs from minus two to one quarter, and it has no gaps. Outside it, every c runs away.
learn.mandel.bar.do: Move c along the bar. Find both ends of the bright part, and see what the answers do just inside and just outside each end.
learn.mandel.bar.name: The bright bar is a picture of a set: the set of every c whose orbit stays close. It is a picture in one dimension, a line. Remember it. The Mandelbrot set is the same picture, made on a flat sheet in place of a line.
learn.mandel.point.title: A number with two parts
learn.mandel.point.text: A number on a line can only go left or right. To get a picture on a sheet, we need numbers that can go up and down as well. So give a number two parts. The first part says how far across it is. The second part says how far up. Together they name one point on the sheet, the way two numbers on a map name one place.
learn.mandel.point.do: Drag the dot. Watch its two parts change. Find the point that is one across and one up.
learn.mandel.point.name: The two parts are called coordinates, and the sheet is called a plane. The idea of naming a point with two numbers comes from René Descartes, nearly four hundred years ago.
learn.mandel.polar.title: Distance and angle
learn.mandel.polar.text: There is a second way to say where a point is. Stand at the middle of the sheet. Say how far away the point is, and which way you have to face to look at it. The way you face is an angle, measured from the line that points right. A quarter turn, ninety degrees, is straight up. A half turn, one hundred and eighty degrees, is straight left. It is the same point, described by a distance and an angle.
learn.mandel.polar.do: Drag the dot round the dashed circle. The distance stays at one and only the angle changes. Then drag it straight outward, and only the distance changes.
learn.mandel.polar.name: Describing a point by its distance and angle is called polar coordinates. The distance comes from the theorem of Pythagoras: square the two parts, add them, and take the square root.
learn.mandel.sqpt.title: Squaring a point
learn.mandel.sqpt.text: How do you multiply a point by itself? The rule is simple when you use distance and angle. Square the distance, and double the angle. That is all. A point on the dashed circle has a distance of one, so its square stays on the circle and only swings round. A point inside the circle moves inward. A point outside moves outward. This is the rule from the number line too. A negative number points left, at a half turn. Doubled, that is a full turn, which points right again. That is why a minus times a minus is a plus.
learn.mandel.sqpt.do: Drag the blue dot. The pink dot is its square. Put the blue dot straight up, one unit from the middle, and see where its square lands.
learn.mandel.sqpt.name: These two-part numbers are called complex numbers. The part across is called the real part, and the part up is called the imaginary part. That is an unlucky name, because it is no more imaginary than a point on a map. The point one unit straight up is called i. Its angle is a quarter turn, so its square sits at a half turn, which is minus one. That is the whole meaning of the famous statement that i squared is minus one.
learn.mandel.add.title: Adding points
learn.mandel.add.text: Adding two points is easier than squaring one. Add the parts across, and add the parts up. In the picture, that means sliding. Start at the first point, then move by the second point's across and up. Wherever you arrive is the sum.
learn.mandel.add.do: Drag the blue dot and the pink dot. The white dot is their sum. Put the pink dot at the middle, and see that adding nothing changes nothing.
learn.mandel.add.name: A point used as a slide, so far across and so far up, is called a vector, and this is vector addition. Complex numbers add in exactly this way.
learn.mandel.onehop.title: The rule on the sheet, one hop at a time
learn.mandel.onehop.text: Now we have everything for the rule from before: square, then add c. This time the numbers are points. Start at the middle. Each hop has two moves. First square the point: square its distance and double its angle. Then add c, which slides it by c's two parts. The dashed line is the squaring. The pink arrow is the slide.
learn.mandel.onehop.do: Press Next hop to add hops one at a time. Follow each one: a dashed line to the square, then a pink arrow that is the same size and points the same way every time. The arithmetic for the hop is written underneath.
learn.mandel.onehop.name: This is the same recurrence as on the line, now with complex numbers. It is usually written as z squared plus c, where z is the point that hops.
learn.mandel.ring.title: The ring of no return
learn.mandel.ring.text: On the line, an answer that got too big ran away. On the sheet the same thing is true, and there is an exact boundary. Draw a ring around the middle with a radius of two. Once a hop lands outside that ring, squaring throws the point so far that adding c can never bring it back. So we can stop following it. For each c there is one question. Do the hops ever leave the ring?
learn.mandel.ring.do: Drag c around. When the hops leave, the first one outside the ring is marked in pink. Find a c that takes more than ten hops to leave. Press Next hop to walk along the path, with the arithmetic for each hop.
learn.mandel.ring.name: The ring is called the escape radius. The number of hops a point takes to leave is called its escape time.
learn.mandel.shapes.title: What the hops do when they stay
learn.mandel.shapes.text: When the hops never leave the ring, they still have to go somewhere. For some values of c they spiral in to a single spot. For others they end up going round two spots, or three, or more, just like the cycles on the line. And close to the border between staying and leaving, the smallest change in c gives a completely different path.
learn.mandel.shapes.do: Press each button to see one spot, two spots and a triangle. Then press the last one, and move c by the smallest amount you can.
learn.mandel.shapes.name: These are the fixed points and cycles from before, now in the complex plane. Places where the tiniest change at the start changes the whole outcome are what people mean by chaos.
learn.mandel.ask.title: One square, one question
learn.mandel.ask.text: Here is how a picture is made from all this. Lay a grid over the sheet. Each square stands for one value of c: the point at the square's middle. Ask the question for that c. If its hops never leave the ring, paint the square black. If they leave, paint it purple. The small window shows the hops for the square you chose. Notice that the hops wander all over the ring. A square's colour does not say where its hops go. It only says whether they got out.
learn.mandel.ask.do: Tap squares to ask them one at a time. Try to guess the colour first. Press Next hop to walk through a square's hops, with the arithmetic for each. Then press the button to ask every square.
learn.mandel.ask.name: A picture where each place stands for a choice, and its colour shows what that choice leads to, is a kind of map. This is a map of c. A square of the grid is what a screen calls a pixel.
learn.mandel.count.title: Count the hops
learn.mandel.count.text: Black or purple is only two answers. We can say more. For each square that leaves the ring, count the hops it took. If it left quickly, paint it a dark colour. If it took longer, paint it brighter. The squares that never leave stay black. Now the picture shows not only whether a square escapes, but how close it came to staying.
learn.mandel.count.do: Watch the squares fill in. Tap a bright one and a dark one, and compare how many hops each took.
learn.mandel.count.name: A picture coloured by the count of hops is called an escape-time picture. Nearly every picture of this shape that you have seen was coloured this way.
learn.mandel.finer.title: A finer grid
learn.mandel.finer.text: The squares so far are big, so the picture is rough. Make them smaller, and there are more questions to ask, but the picture gets sharper. Nobody draws the shape that appears. It is only the same small question, asked once for every square. Look along the middle of the picture from left to right. It is the bright bar from before, from minus two to one quarter.
learn.mandel.finer.do: Make the grid finer one step at a time, and watch the shape appear. The finest grid asks more than a hundred and sixty thousand questions.
learn.mandel.finer.name: The black shape is the Mandelbrot set: every c whose orbit never escapes. It is named after Benoit Mandelbrot, who studied it with a computer in 1980.
learn.mandel.patience.title: How long to wait before giving up
learn.mandel.patience.text: The black shape is every c that never leaves the ring. But a computer cannot wait for never. It can only count up to some limit and then give up. Set the limit to one hop, and everything inside the ring counts as staying. Raise the limit, and each extra hop carves a little more away. The true shape is what remains when the limit grows without end. Every picture of it, however fine, is only the best guess so far.
learn.mandel.patience.do: Start with the limit at one, and raise it one hop at a time. Watch the ring turn into the shape.
learn.mandel.patience.name: A value that is approached as a count grows without end is called a limit, and it is the idea underneath calculus. The exact area of the Mandelbrot set is still not known. It is about one and a half, and nobody has found a formula for it.
learn.r.one: Stays close: it settles on one place.
learn.r.many: Stays close: it visits {0} places in turn.
learn.r.none: Stays close, with no simple pattern.
learn.r.limit: Black: has not left the ring after {0} hops.
learn.r.landIn: lands on ({0}, {1}), {2} from the middle: inside the ring
learn.r.landOut: lands on ({0}, {1}), {2} from the middle: outside the ring
learn.r.byParts: the same, worked from the two parts
learn.track.space: From a flat picture to a world you can fly through
learn.space.ray.title: One line of sight for each square
learn.space.ray.text: The Mandelbrot picture was a grid of squares, and each square was asked one question. A picture of a world is made the same way, with a different question. Start with a flat world, seen here from above. There is an eye at the bottom, and some round pillars. In front of the eye is a row of squares. That row is the picture. For each square, draw a straight line from the eye through the square and on into the world. Whatever that line hits first is what the square shows.
learn.space.ray.do: Drag across the drawing to choose a square, and watch where its line goes. The row along the top is the picture the eye would see.
learn.space.ray.name: A line of sight is called a ray, and making a picture this way is called ray casting. The row of squares is the screen. A flat world gives a picture that is only one row. A world with depth gives the whole grid, and we will get there.
learn.space.safe.title: How far is the nearest thing?
learn.space.safe.text: How do we find what a line hits? There is a trick, and it starts with one question. Stand anywhere in the world and ask: how far away is the nearest thing? Not in which direction. Only how far. That one number draws a circle around you, and inside the circle there is nothing at all. So you can move that far, in any direction you like, and be sure of not hitting anything.
learn.space.safe.do: Drag the dot around. The circle is the room you have. Find the place with the most room.
learn.space.safe.name: A rule that gives, for every place, the distance to the nearest thing is called a distance function. With several things, it is the smallest of their distances, which is called the minimum.
learn.space.march.title: Walk the line in safe moves
learn.space.march.text: Now walk along a line of sight. Ask how far the nearest thing is, and move exactly that far along the line. You cannot have hit anything, because you had that much room. Ask again from the new place, and move again. Far from everything, the moves are long. Close to a pillar, they get short. When the room left is almost nothing, you have arrived at a surface. If you get a long way out and still have room, the line hit nothing.
learn.space.march.do: Press Next move to walk the line one move at a time. Then choose a line that only just misses a pillar, and count how many moves it takes.
learn.space.march.name: This way of walking is called sphere tracing, or ray marching. It was described by John Hart in 1996. Every world in Mirrorfold is drawn with it.
learn.space.row.title: Paint the row
learn.space.row.text: Do that walk for every square in the row. Each square gets one number: how far its line went before it arrived. Paint a square bright if its line arrived soon, dim if it went a long way, and black if it hit nothing. That is already a picture. Near things are bright, far things are dim, and the edges of the pillars show up as sudden changes.
learn.space.row.do: Make the row finer. Then choose squares on each side of a pillar's edge, and compare how far their lines went.
learn.space.row.name: The distance along each line of sight is called depth, and a picture painted with it is called a depth map.
learn.space.ball.title: The distance to a round pillar
learn.space.ball.text: Where does the distance number come from? Not from measuring. It is worked out with a sum. Take one round pillar at the middle of the sheet. First find how far you are from its middle. That is the rule from the first track: square your two parts, add them, and take the square root. Then take away the pillar's radius. What is left is the gap between you and its surface.
learn.space.ball.do: Drag the dot and follow the sum underneath. Then drag it inside the pillar, and see what the sum says.
learn.space.ball.name: This is the distance function of a circle. Inside the shape the answer goes below zero, and it says how deep inside you are. A distance that can be negative like this is called a signed distance.
learn.space.hollow.title: Turn it inside out
learn.space.hollow.text: Now swap the two sides. Let everything be solid rock, and let the circle be a bubble of empty space inside it. The sum turns round too. Take the bubble's radius, and take away your distance from its middle. Inside the bubble, the answer is how much room you have before you reach the wall. Out in the rock, it is below zero.
learn.space.hollow.do: Drag the dot around inside the bubble. Find where the room is greatest, and what it is at the very edge.
learn.space.hollow.name: Swapping inside and outside is done by changing the sign of the distance. The new shape is called the complement of the old one.
learn.space.repeat.title: One bubble in every cell
learn.space.repeat.text: One bubble is not much of a world. Here is how to get endlessly many, for the price of one. Cut the sheet into square cells, two units wide. Before doing the bubble sum, replace your position with your position inside your own cell. That is a remainder: divide by two and keep what is left over. Then take away one, so that the middle of the cell counts as zero. Now every cell runs the same sum, so every cell has its own bubble.
learn.space.repeat.do: Drag the dot from one cell into the next, and watch the remainder start again from the beginning.
learn.space.repeat.name: Keeping the remainder after a division is called the modulo operation. It is the arithmetic of a clock, where the hours start again after twelve. Repeating a shape this way costs nothing extra, however many copies there are.
learn.space.join.title: Bubbles that join up
learn.space.join.text: While the bubbles are small, each one is a closed room, and there is no way out of it. Make them bigger. When the radius passes one, which is half the width of a cell, each bubble breaks through into its neighbours. Now the empty space is all one piece, and it goes on for ever in every direction. What is left of the rock is a pattern of pillars.
learn.space.join.do: Move the slider slowly past one, and watch the walls open. Then try 1.25, which is the size the Foam world uses.
learn.space.join.name: A space that is all in one piece is called connected. Because the pattern repeats exactly, the world has no edge to fall off, and a traveller can never tell one cell from the next. A pattern like that is called periodic.
learn.space.small.title: The same thing, three times smaller
learn.space.small.text: Next, a second set of bubbles, three times smaller than the first. There is no need for a new sum. Multiply your position by three, and run the same sum as before. That gives the answer for a world three times bigger than we want. So divide the answer by three as well. The result is the same pattern, shrunk to a third of its size.
learn.space.small.do: Drag the dot and follow the sum. The last line divides by three, to bring the answer back to our size.
learn.space.small.name: Shrinking or growing a shape without changing its form is called scaling, and two shapes that differ only in size are called similar.
learn.space.both.title: Big bubbles and small bubbles together
learn.space.both.text: Now use both sets at once. At any place, the big bubbles give one number for how much room you have, and the small bubbles give another. You are in empty space if either of them says so. And the room you really have is the larger of the two numbers. So work out both, and keep the larger. The small bubbles eat into the rock that the big ones left behind.
learn.space.both.do: The drawing is a close view of one pillar of rock, with a big bubble at each corner. Drag the dot into a small bubble inside the pillar. See which of the two numbers wins there, and which wins in a big bubble.
learn.space.both.name: Keeping the larger of two numbers is called taking the maximum. Empty space that belongs to one set of bubbles or the other is called their union.
learn.space.levels.title: Again and again
learn.space.levels.text: There is no reason to stop at two sizes. Add a third set of bubbles, three times smaller again, and a fourth. Each set uses the same sum, with the position multiplied by three once more, and the largest answer is kept. The shape now has detail at four different sizes, and it was all made by one short sum used four times.
learn.space.levels.do: Add the levels one at a time. The drawing is a close view of one pillar of rock: watch what each level does to it.
learn.space.levels.name: A shape with detail at every size, made by repeating one rule at smaller and smaller scales, is called a fractal. Repeating a rule is iteration, the same idea that made the Mandelbrot set.
learn.space.third.title: A third number
learn.space.third.text: So far the world has been flat. To give it depth, give every point a third number. The first says how far across. The second says how far up. The third says how far forward, away from you. The sums hardly change. To find the distance from the middle, square all three parts, add them, and take the square root. So the bubble sum works in a world with depth, and a bubble becomes a hollow ball.
learn.space.third.do: Move the three sliders, and follow the distance sum. Find a point that is exactly three units from the middle.
learn.space.third.name: A world where a point needs three numbers is called three-dimensional. The distance sum is the theorem of Pythagoras, used with three parts in place of two. The surface of a ball is called a sphere.
learn.space.picture.title: A picture of a world with depth
learn.space.picture.text: Now put it all together. The eye is inside a world of bubbles at four sizes, with depth. The picture is a grid of squares again, because the eye can look up and down as well as left and right. Each square has its own line of sight. Walk each line in safe moves until it arrives at a wall, and paint the square by how far it went. Near walls are bright, and far ones are dim.
learn.space.picture.do: Make the grid finer and watch the world appear. Tap a square, then press Next move to walk its line.
learn.space.picture.name: This world is the one called Foam in Mirrorfold. Making a picture from a description of a world is called rendering.
learn.space.facing.title: Which way does a wall face?
learn.space.facing.text: The picture so far shows how far away each wall is, but not its shape. For that we need to know which way each bit of wall is facing. The distance number can tell us. Stand near a wall. Take a tiny step to the right and see how much room you have there. Do the same to the left, and up, and down. The direction in which the room grows fastest points straight out of the wall.
learn.space.facing.do: Drag the dot close to a wall. Follow the small sums, and see that the arrow always points directly away from the nearest wall.
learn.space.facing.name: The direction in which a number grows fastest is called its gradient, and the arrow that sticks straight out of a surface is called its normal. Measuring how fast something changes over a tiny step is the central idea of calculus.
learn.space.lamp.title: Light from a lamp
learn.space.lamp.text: Now add a lamp, far away, so that its light arrives from one direction. A bit of surface that faces the lamp squarely is brightly lit. A bit that is turned sideways to it catches less light. A bit that faces away catches none. To measure how well two arrows line up, multiply their across parts, multiply their up parts, and add the two answers. Arrows that point the same way give one. Arrows at right angles give zero.
learn.space.lamp.do: Drag the pink lamp around the pillar. Then drag the blue dot around the surface, and follow the sum for its brightness.
learn.space.lamp.name: That sum is called the dot product of the two arrows. The rule that brightness depends on it is Lambert's law, from 1760. For arrows one unit long, the dot product is the cosine of the angle between them.
learn.space.lit.title: The lit picture
learn.space.lit.text: Do that for every square. Each line of sight arrives at a wall. Find which way the wall faces there, compare it with the direction of the lamp, and that gives the brightness. Then dim it a little for distance, as before. Now the bubbles look round, because the brightness changes smoothly across each curved wall.
learn.space.lit.do: Move the lamp with the slider, and watch the light slide across the walls. Tap a wall to see the sum for its brightness.
learn.space.lit.name: Working out the brightness of a surface from its direction and the light is called shading. Mirrorfold adds colour, glow and fog on top, but underneath it is this.
learn.space.fly.title: Move the eye, and you are flying
learn.space.fly.text: A picture like this is one moment. Move the eye a little way forward and make the picture again, and it has changed a little. Do that sixty times a second and you are flying. A phone can do it because its graphics chip asks every square its question at the same time. And because the world repeats every two units, the eye can go forward for ever and never reach an edge.
learn.space.fly.do: Slide the eye forward. When it has gone two units, compare the picture with the one you started from. Then press the button to fly through this world yourself.
learn.space.fly.name: Each picture is called a frame. Making them as fast as they are shown is called real-time rendering, and the small program the graphics chip runs for every square is called a shader.
learn.fly: Close the lessons and fly through this world

learn.r.tap: Tap a square to see its hops.
learn.track.worlds: How the other worlds are made
learn.deeper.zoom.title: Look closer
learn.deeper.zoom.text: The edge of the Mandelbrot set looks rough. So look closer, and see whether it gets smooth. Looking closer costs nothing new. The squares of the grid simply stand for places that are nearer together, and each one is asked the same question as before. However close you look, the edge never becomes smooth. There are always more curls, and curls on those.
learn.deeper.zoom.do: Move the slider to magnify the picture, a doubling at a time. The small cross marks the place the picture is closing in on.
learn.deeper.zoom.name: A shape that stays just as rough however closely you look is called a fractal. Near the edge, a point takes many hops to make up its mind, so the limit on the count has to rise as you go in.
learn.deeper.baby.title: Small copies of the whole
learn.deeper.baby.text: Now close in on a different place, far out on the thin spike at the left. In the first track, setting c to minus 1.755 made the answers visit three places in turn. Look closely at that very spot, and there is a tiny copy of the whole Mandelbrot set sitting on the spike. It is not a perfect copy, but it has the same body, the same head, and the same buds. There are endlessly many of these, all through the edge.
learn.deeper.baby.do: Magnify until the small copy fills the picture. Then press the button to fly into the Mandelbrot set yourself.
learn.deeper.baby.name: A shape that contains small copies of itself is called self-similar. The small copies are sometimes called minibrots. Their middles are exactly the values of c whose orbit comes back to zero.
learn.deeper.start.title: Keep c, and change where you start
learn.deeper.start.text: Until now every path started at the middle, and each square of the picture was a different c. Turn that round. Choose one c and keep it. Let each square of the picture be a place to start from. Square and add c from there, and ask the same question: do the hops ever leave the ring? This time the hops do belong on the picture, because its squares are places, and the hops move among them.
learn.deeper.start.do: Tap the picture to choose a starting place, and watch its hops. Then press the buttons to change c. With c at zero the black shape is a plain disc, because squaring alone shrinks anything closer than one.
learn.deeper.start.name: The black shape is called a filled Julia set, after Gaston Julia, who studied these in 1918, long before there were computers to draw them. Every value of c has its own.
learn.deeper.map.title: The Mandelbrot set is a map of them all
learn.deeper.map.text: Every c has its own Julia picture, so there are endlessly many of them. The small picture in the corner is the Mandelbrot set, and the pink dot on it is c. Drag the dot and the big picture changes. While c is inside the black of the Mandelbrot set, the Julia picture is in one piece. When c crosses outside, the picture falls apart into dust. So the Mandelbrot set is a map. It shows, for every c at once, which kind of Julia picture that c has.
learn.deeper.map.do: Drag c slowly across the edge of the small black shape, and watch the big picture break up. Then drag it into one of the round buds, and count the arms where the pieces meet.
learn.deeper.map.name: A shape in one piece is called connected. The Mandelbrot set is the set of all c whose Julia set is connected. That is its definition, and it is why the first track always started its hops from the middle.
learn.deeper.power.title: Change the rule
learn.deeper.power.text: Squaring a point squared its distance and doubled its angle. What if the rule tripled the angle, and cubed the distance? That is multiplying the point by itself three times. Everything else stays the same: add c, repeat, and ask whether the hops leave the ring. The picture changes, but in an orderly way. Doubling the angle gave a shape with one body. Tripling it gives two, and four times the angle gives three.
learn.deeper.power.do: Raise the power one at a time, and count the bodies each time.
learn.deeper.power.name: The number of times a point is multiplied by itself is called the power, or the degree, of the rule. A shape that looks the same after part of a turn has rotational symmetry.
learn.deeper.ship.title: Fold before you square
learn.deeper.ship.text: Here is one more change to the rule, and it is a small one. Before each squaring, make both parts of the point positive: throw away their minus signs. Then square and add c as usual. That one extra move breaks the smooth round buds into something that looks like a ship on fire, with masts and rigging.
learn.deeper.ship.do: Compare this picture with the Mandelbrot set. Look for the small ships along the line to the left of the big one.
learn.deeper.ship.name: Throwing away a minus sign is called taking the absolute value. On the sheet it folds everything into one corner, like folding a piece of paper in four. This picture is called the Burning Ship, and it was found in 1992. It is the same fold that makes the mirrors in the track on the other worlds.
learn.worlds.mirror.title: A mirror is a thrown-away minus sign
learn.worlds.mirror.text: The second track built a world out of bubbles. Most of Mirrorfold's other worlds are built with mirrors, and a mirror is the simplest sum there is. Here is one round pillar, to the right of the middle. Before working out the distance to it, throw away the minus sign of your across part. Now a place on the left gets exactly the same answer as the matching place on the right. So a second pillar appears on the left, for free.
learn.worlds.mirror.do: Drag the dot from the right side to the left, and watch the sum. The across part loses its sign, and everything after that is the same.
learn.worlds.mirror.name: Throwing away the minus sign is called taking the absolute value. It folds the sheet in half along the upright line, and a shape that matches its own mirror image is called symmetric.
learn.worlds.mirror2.title: Two mirrors
learn.worlds.mirror2.text: Do the same to the up part as well. Now the sheet is folded in half twice, like a piece of paper folded in four, and one pillar has become four. The sum has hardly grown. Two minus signs are thrown away, and then it is the same distance sum as for a single pillar.
learn.worlds.mirror2.do: Drag the dot into each of the four corners in turn. See that the sum always ends up measuring to the one real pillar, at the top right.
learn.worlds.mirror2.name: Two mirrors at right angles give a pattern that looks the same when turned by half a turn. Each fold doubles the number of copies, so ten folds would give more than a thousand pillars for the price of one.
learn.worlds.turn.title: Turn the sheet first
learn.worlds.turn.text: Mirrors that only run straight across and straight up make everything square. To get other angles, turn the sheet before folding it. Turning a place needs two numbers that come from the angle, called its cosine and its sine. The new across part is the old across times the cosine, plus the old up times the sine. The new up part is the old up times the cosine, take away the old across times the sine. Then fold as before.
learn.worlds.turn.do: Move the slider to turn the pattern. At ninety degrees it looks the same as at zero, because the four pillars swap places.
learn.worlds.turn.name: Turning about a point is called a rotation. The cosine of an angle is the across part of the point on the circle at that angle, and the sine is its up part.
learn.worlds.kale.title: A kaleidoscope
learn.worlds.kale.text: A kaleidoscope is two mirrors at an angle, and it can be done with one sum using distance and angle from the first track. Work out the angle of your place. Then fold that angle back and forth until it lies inside one thin wedge. Whatever stands in that wedge appears in all the others, turned and mirrored. The Mirrors button in Mirrorfold does exactly this to the direction you are looking.
learn.worlds.kale.do: Press the buttons to change the number of mirrors. Drag the dot round the middle, and watch its folded angle go up and down between zero and the width of the wedge.
learn.worlds.kale.name: A pattern made by mirrors meeting at a point has dihedral symmetry. The kaleidoscope was invented by David Brewster in 1816.
learn.worlds.box.title: The distance to a block
learn.worlds.box.text: Bubbles and pillars are round. For walls and corridors we need a block with flat sides, and folding gives one. Throw away both minus signs, so that only one corner of the block is left to think about. Then take away the block's half width from your across part, and its half height from your up part. Each answer is a gap, to one pair of sides. The larger of the two is the room you have.
learn.worlds.box.do: Drag the dot around the block, and watch which of the two gaps is the larger. Then drag it out past a corner.
learn.worlds.box.name: Out past a corner the real distance is a little more than this sum says. That does no harm. A safe move may be too short, but it must never be too long. An answer that is never too big is called a lower bound.
learn.worlds.carpet.title: Holes inside holes
learn.worlds.carpet.text: Now put the pieces together. Take a square block. Cut a square hole in its middle, a third as wide. Then cut the block into nine, and cut a hole a third as wide in the middle of each ninth. Then do it again, three times smaller. Every level uses the same sum: a remainder to find your place in your own cell, a fold to measure to the square hole, and a division to shrink it. The largest answer is kept, as with the bubbles.
learn.worlds.carpet.do: Add the sizes of hole one at a time. Drag the dot into a hole, and see which level's number is the largest there.
learn.worlds.carpet.name: This shape is called the Sierpinski carpet, described by Wacław Sierpiński in 1916. If the cutting went on for ever, there would be no area left at all, and yet the edges of the holes would have endless length.
learn.worlds.sponge.title: The carpet with depth
learn.worlds.sponge.text: Give the carpet depth, and cut the square holes through it in all three directions. This is the world called Sponge. The picture is made exactly as in the second track. Each square has a line of sight, walked in safe moves, using the block and hole sums with three parts in place of two. In Mirrorfold you fly along the square tunnels that the holes leave.
learn.worlds.sponge.do: Move the lamp, and tap a wall to see the sum for its brightness. Then press the button to fly through it.
learn.worlds.sponge.name: With depth the shape is called the Menger sponge, after Karl Menger, who described it in 1926. It has endless surface, and no volume at all.
learn.worlds.bulb.title: The Mandelbrot rule, with depth
learn.worlds.bulb.text: One more world, and it joins the first track to the second. Take the Mandelbrot rule, and use it on points with depth. A place on the sheet had a distance and one angle. A place with depth has a distance and two angles, like a place on the Earth, which has a longitude and a latitude. So raise the distance to a power, multiply both angles by the same number, add c, and repeat. The shape is every c whose hops never leave. Mirrorfold fills a world with them.
learn.worlds.bulb.do: Move the lamp to see the shape of the surface. Then press the button to fly among them.
learn.worlds.bulb.name: This shape is called the Mandelbulb. It was found by Daniel White and Paul Nylander in 2009. Describing a point by a distance and two angles is called spherical coordinates.
learn.look.rgb.title: A colour is three numbers
learn.look.rgb.text: A screen has only three colours of light: red, green and blue. Every colour you see on it is a mixture of those three, each one somewhere between off and full. So a colour is three numbers. Red and green together make yellow. All three together make white. All three at the same middle value make grey.
learn.look.rgb.do: Move the three sliders and mix some colours. Then try to make orange without looking at the buttons.
learn.look.rgb.name: Making colours by adding lights together is called additive mixing, and the three numbers are called the red, green and blue components of the colour.
learn.look.wave.title: A wave from a circle
learn.look.wave.text: A palette needs a number that rises and falls smoothly, over and over. There is one in the first track already. Take a point going round a circle, and watch only its across part. As the angle grows, the across part goes from one, down through zero to minus one, and back up to one. Draw that number against the angle and it makes a wave.
learn.look.wave.do: Move the slider and watch the pink line on the circle and the pink line on the graph. They are the same length. Find the angles where the wave crosses zero.
learn.look.wave.name: This number is called the cosine of the angle. A wave that repeats exactly, for ever, is called periodic, and one full repeat is called a cycle.
learn.look.amp.title: Lift it and size it
learn.look.amp.text: The cosine wave runs from minus one to plus one, but a colour needs a number from zero to one. So change the wave with two sums. Multiply it by a size, which makes it taller or flatter. Then add a middle value, which lifts the whole wave up or down. With a middle of a half and a size of a half, the wave runs exactly from zero to one.
learn.look.amp.do: Move the two sliders. The strip under the graph shows the wave as brightness. Make a wave that stays between a quarter and three quarters.
learn.look.amp.name: The size of a wave is called its amplitude, and the value it rises and falls around is called its offset.
learn.look.freq.title: Squeeze it and slide it
learn.look.freq.text: Two more sums change the wave sideways. Multiply the position by a number before taking the cosine, and the wave is squeezed, so that more repeats fit in the same space. Add a number to the position, and the whole wave slides along. Those are all four ways to change a wave: its middle, its size, how many times it repeats, and where it starts.
learn.look.freq.do: Squeeze the wave until it repeats three times. Then slide it by a half, and see that the bright parts and the dark parts have swapped.
learn.look.freq.name: How many times a wave repeats is called its frequency, and how far along it has been slid is called its phase.
learn.look.palette.title: Three waves make a palette
learn.look.palette.text: Now use three waves, one for red, one for green and one for blue. Go along the strip from left to right. At each place the three waves give three numbers, and three numbers are a colour. If the three waves are slid by different amounts, they take turns being bright, and the strip runs through many colours. Every palette in Mirrorfold is made this way. It is twelve numbers: a middle, a size, a repeat and a slide for each of the three waves.
learn.look.palette.do: Press the buttons to see some of Mirrorfold's own palettes. Then move the three sliders to slide each wave, and make a palette of your own. Drag across the drawing to read the sum at any place.
learn.look.palette.name: A rule that turns one number into a colour is called a palette, or a colour map. This way of making one from cosines was described by the programmer Inigo Quilez.
learn.look.paint.title: Colour the picture with it
learn.look.paint.text: Here is the Mandelbrot picture again, with a palette. Each square has its count of hops. Divide the count by a number, to turn it into a position along the palette, and paint the square the colour found there. Squares with nearly the same count get nearly the same colour, which is why the colours run in bands. Add a little to every position and all the colours move along together. Mirrorfold does that slowly all the time, and it is why its colours drift.
learn.look.paint.do: Move the slider to slide the colours. Press the buttons to change the palette. Tap a square to see how its colour was worked out.
learn.look.paint.name: Turning a number into a colour by looking it up along a palette is called colour mapping. Sliding the colours over time is called colour cycling.
learn.look.fade.title: A picture that remembers
learn.look.fade.text: Mirrorfold's trails come from one idea. Do not start each new picture from black. Start it from the picture before, made a little darker. Then draw the new things on top. Something that was drawn one picture ago is still there, slightly dimmer. Something from ten pictures ago is dimmer still. So everything that moves leaves a trail behind it, fading away.
learn.look.fade.do: Move the slider to change how much of the old picture is kept. Watch the trails get longer and shorter.
learn.look.fade.name: Using the last result as part of the next one is called feedback. Multiplying by the same number again and again is called exponential decay, and it is how hot things cool and how sounds die away.
learn.look.grow.title: Make the memory bigger
learn.look.grow.text: Now do one more thing to the old picture before drawing on it. Make it a tiny bit bigger. Every time a new picture is made, everything already in it moves a little further from the middle. So the trails no longer stay where they were left. They fly outward, and it looks as if you are rushing forward through a tunnel. Make the old picture a tiny bit smaller, and the trails fall inward.
learn.look.grow.do: Move the slider either side of one. Find the value where the trails neither fly out nor fall in.
learn.look.grow.name: Making a picture bigger or smaller is called scaling. A change of one part in a hundred, repeated sixty times a second, nearly doubles the size every second. Growth like that is called exponential growth.
learn.look.spin.title: Turn the memory
learn.look.spin.text: Add one more small change. As well as making the old picture a little bigger, turn it by a small angle. Each trail is now pushed outward and round at the same time, and it becomes a spiral. Turning and growing together is something the first track met already. It is what multiplying by a two-part number does: it multiplies the distance and adds to the angle.
learn.look.spin.do: Move the slider to turn the old picture one way or the other. Set it to zero to get the straight tunnel back.
learn.look.spin.name: A curve that turns by the same angle each time it grows by the same amount is called a logarithmic spiral. Snail shells and the arms of galaxies have this shape.
learn.look.motions.title: Mirrorfold's motions
learn.look.motions.text: Mirrorfold's Motion button chooses between sets of these numbers. Each motion says how much of the old picture to keep, how much bigger or smaller to make it, and how far to turn it. Some motions add a wobble or a ripple, which push different parts of the old picture by different amounts, but the idea is the same. The world is drawn fresh sixty times a second, and the trails are only the old pictures, faded and moved.
learn.look.motions.do: Press each button to load one of Mirrorfold's motions, and read its three numbers underneath.
learn.look.motions.name: A set of changes applied to a whole picture, such as growing, turning and sliding, is called a transformation.
learn.look.neg.title: A rule for every square
learn.look.neg.text: A filter is a rule that is used on every square of a finished picture. The simplest is the negative. A colour is three numbers from zero to one. Take each of them away from one. Bright becomes dark, dark becomes bright, and red becomes its opposite, which is a pale blue-green. The rule knows nothing about what is in the picture. It only sees one square's three numbers at a time.
learn.look.neg.do: Move the slider from none of the filter to all of it. Tap a square to see the sum for its red part.
learn.look.neg.name: A rule that changes each square using only that square's own colour is called a point operation. The colour that a negative turns another into is called its complement.
learn.look.fewer.title: Fewer shades
learn.look.fewer.text: Each of a colour's three numbers can take any value from zero to one. This filter allows only a few. Multiply the number by how many levels there are, throw away everything after the decimal point, and scale it back. Every shade is pushed down to the nearest level below it. With only two levels for each of red, green and blue, the whole picture is made of eight colours.
learn.look.fewer.do: Move the slider from many levels down to two, and watch the smooth bands turn into flat patches.
learn.look.fewer.name: Throwing away the part after the decimal point is called rounding down. Limiting a number to a few fixed levels is called quantising, and a picture treated this way is said to be posterised.
learn.look.mosaic.title: Round the position
learn.look.mosaic.text: The last filter rounded off the colour. This one rounds off the position. Cut the picture into blocks. Every square in a block takes its colour from the one square at the block's middle. Nothing new is worked out. Each square only looks somewhere else for its colour. The picture turns into large tiles.
learn.look.mosaic.do: Make the blocks bigger and smaller. Tap a square to see which square it takes its colour from.
learn.look.mosaic.name: Taking one value to stand for a whole area is called sampling. The number of separate squares in a picture is called its resolution, and this filter lowers it.
learn.look.bulge.title: Look somewhere else
learn.look.bulge.text: A square does not have to show the colour that belongs at its own place. It can show the colour from anywhere. This filter makes each square near the middle look for its colour closer to the middle than it really is. So the middle of the picture is spread out over a larger area, and the picture seems to bulge toward you. Turn the number the other way, and it pinches inward.
learn.look.bulge.do: Move the slider both ways from zero. Tap a square: the pink dot is the place its colour comes from.
learn.look.bulge.name: A rule that says where each square should look for its colour is called a mapping, or a warp. A glass lens does the same to light, and Mirrorfold's VR viewer uses a warp like this one to cancel the bend of its lenses.
learn.look.blur.title: Average the neighbours
learn.look.blur.text: A square can also look at more than one place. To blur a picture, give each square the average of all the squares around it. Add up their numbers, and divide by how many there are. Sharp edges are smeared, because a square on an edge averages some bright neighbours with some dark ones. Mirrorfold's glow is made this way. The bright parts of the picture are blurred, and the blurred copy is added back on top.
learn.look.blur.do: Move the slider to average over a wider and wider area.
learn.look.blur.name: Adding numbers up and dividing by how many there are gives their average, or mean. A filter that mixes each square with its neighbours is called a convolution.
learn.look.edge.title: Differences find the edges
learn.look.edge.text: Averaging the neighbours hides edges. Taking them away from each other finds edges. For each square, take the square to its right and the square to its left, and find the difference between them. Do the same for the squares above and below. In a flat patch of colour the differences are nearly nothing, so the square is dark. Where the colour changes suddenly, they are large, so the square is bright. Only the outlines are left.
learn.look.edge.do: Move the slider from the plain picture to edges only. Tap a square on an outline and one in a flat patch, and compare their sums.
learn.look.edge.name: The difference between neighbours measures how fast the picture is changing from place to place. It is the same idea as the tiny steps that found which way a wall faces, and it is where calculus begins.
learn.look.sound.title: Sound is a wave
learn.look.sound.text: Sound is air being pushed and pulled, very quickly. Draw the push against time and it is a wave, like the waves of the palette. Two things about the wave are heard. How many times it repeats in a second is its pitch: more repeats sound higher. How tall it is gives its loudness.
learn.look.sound.do: Move the two sliders, and say what the sound would do: go higher, go lower, get louder or get quieter.
learn.look.sound.name: The number of repeats in a second is called the frequency, and it is measured in hertz. The lowest note of a piano repeats about 27 times a second, and the highest about 4,000 times.
learn.look.mix.title: Adding waves
learn.look.mix.text: Music is many waves at once. When two sounds reach your ear together, their pushes simply add. Here are three waves: a slow one for the bass, a quicker one for the middle, and a fast one for the treble. The thick line is their sum, worked out moment by moment. It looks complicated, but nothing is lost. The three simple waves are all still in there.
learn.look.mix.do: Change the three amounts and watch the thick line. Drag across the drawing to choose a moment, and read the sum for it.
learn.look.mix.name: Waves adding together without disturbing one another is called superposition. Joseph Fourier showed in 1822 that any repeating wave at all can be built by adding simple ones.
learn.look.bands.title: Taking a sound apart
learn.look.bands.text: Mirrorfold hears only the thick line: one complicated wave. To react to the bass and the treble separately, it has to take the mixture apart again. Here is how. To find how much of the slow wave is in the mixture, multiply the mixture by a pure slow wave, moment by moment, and average the answers. The other waves cancel out, and what is left is the amount of the slow one. The bars show the three amounts found this way.
learn.look.bands.do: Change the three sliders. The bars are not copied from the sliders. They are measured from the thick line, and they come out the same.
learn.look.bands.name: Finding the amount of each frequency in a wave is called a Fourier transform, and the list of amounts is called the spectrum. A range of frequencies taken together is called a band.
learn.look.drive.title: One number pushes another
learn.look.drive.text: Now join the sound to the picture. Mirrorfold measures the bass sixty times a second and gets one number, which is large on a beat and small between beats. That number can be added to any other number in the picture. Here it is added to how much the old picture grows. On each beat the trails are pushed outward a little harder, so the whole picture breathes in time with the music. The pulse here is slow and soft on purpose. Nothing in Mirrorfold is allowed to flash.
learn.look.drive.do: Move the slider to change how hard the pulse pushes. Set it to zero, and the pulse is still there, but it changes nothing.
learn.look.drive.name: Letting one changing number control another is called modulation. So the whole picture is arithmetic: a world from distance sums, colour from three waves, trails from memory, and sound from taking a wave apart.
